> ## Documentation Index
> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/llms.txt
> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# Connect to local MCP servers

> Learn how to extend Claude Desktop with local MCP servers to enable file system access and other powerful integrations

Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers extend AI applications' capabilities by providing secure, controlled access to local resources and tools. Many clients support MCP, enabling diverse integration possibilities across different platforms and applications.

This guide demonstrates how to connect to local MCP servers using Claude Desktop as an example, one of the many clients that support MCP. While we focus on Claude Desktop's implementation, the concepts apply broadly to other MCP-compatible clients. By the end of this tutorial, Claude will be able to interact with files on your computer, create new documents, organize folders, and search through your file system—all with your explicit permission for each action.

![Claude Desktop with filesystem integration showing file management capabilities](https://mintcdn.com/mcp/4ZXF1PrDkEaJvXpn/images/quickstart-filesystem.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=4ZXF1PrDkEaJvXpn\&q=85\&s=629d7e754dc358d71a408d6ce970c1b1)

## Prerequisites

Before starting this tutorial, ensure you have the following installed on your system:

### Claude Desktop

Download and install [Claude Desktop](https://claude.ai/download) for your operating system. Claude Desktop is available for macOS, Windows, and Linux.

If you already have Claude Desktop installed, verify you're running the latest version by clicking the Claude menu and selecting "Check for Updates..."

### Node.js

The Filesystem Server and many other MCP servers require Node.js to run. Verify your Node.js installation by opening a terminal or command prompt and running:

```bash theme={null}
node --version
```

If Node.js is not installed, download it from [nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org/). We recommend the LTS (Long Term Support) version for stability.

## Understanding MCP Servers

MCP servers are programs that run on your computer and provide specific capabilities to Claude Desktop through a standardized protocol. Each server exposes tools that Claude can use to perform actions, with your approval. The Filesystem Server we'll install provides tools for:

* Reading file contents and directory structures
* Creating new files and directories
* Moving and renaming files
* Searching for files by name or content

All actions require your explicit approval before execution, ensuring you maintain full control over what Claude can access and modify.

## Installing the Filesystem Server

The process involves configuring Claude Desktop to automatically start the Filesystem Server whenever you launch the application. This configuration is done through a JSON file that tells Claude Desktop which servers to run and how to connect to them.

**1. Open Claude Desktop Settings**

Start by accessing the Claude Desktop settings. Click on the Claude menu in your system's menu bar (not the settings within the Claude window itself) and select "Settings..."

On macOS, this appears in the top menu bar:

![Claude Desktop menu showing Settings option](https://mintcdn.com/mcp/4ZXF1PrDkEaJvXpn/images/quickstart-menu.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=4ZXF1PrDkEaJvXpn\&q=85\&s=0c8b57e0e17af3624b6762a3ea944c8e)

This opens the Claude Desktop configuration window, which is separate from your Claude account settings.

**2. Access Developer Settings**

In the Settings window, navigate to the "Developer" tab in the left sidebar. This section contains options for configuring MCP servers and other developer features.

Click the "Edit Config" button to open the configuration file:

![Developer settings showing Edit Config button](https://mintcdn.com/mcp/4ZXF1PrDkEaJvXpn/images/quickstart-developer.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=4ZXF1PrDkEaJvXpn\&q=85\&s=0fb595490a2f9e15c0301e771a57446c)

This action creates a new configuration file if one doesn't exist, or opens your existing configuration. The file is located at:

* **macOS**: `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`
* **Windows**: `%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json`
* **Linux**: `~/.config/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`

**3. Configure the Filesystem Server**

Replace the contents of the configuration file with the following JSON structure. This configuration tells Claude Desktop to start the Filesystem Server with access to specific directories:

```json macOS theme={null}
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "filesystem": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "-y",
        "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem",
        "/Users/username/Desktop",
        "/Users/username/Downloads"
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

```json Windows theme={null}
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "filesystem": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "-y",
        "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem",
        "C:\\Users\\username\\Desktop",
        "C:\\Users\\username\\Downloads"
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

Replace `username` with your actual computer username. The paths listed in the `args` array specify which directories the Filesystem Server can access. You can modify these paths or add additional directories as needed.

> [!TIP]
>
> **Understanding the Configuration**
>
> * `"filesystem"`: A friendly name for the server that appears in Claude Desktop
> * `"command": "npx"`: Uses Node.js's npx tool to run the server
> * `"-y"`: Automatically confirms the installation of the server package
> * `"@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem"`: The package name of the Filesystem Server
> * The remaining arguments: Directories the server is allowed to access

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Security Consideration**
>
> Only grant access to directories you're comfortable with Claude reading and modifying. The server runs with your user account permissions, so it can perform any file operations you can perform manually.

**4. Restart Claude Desktop**

After saving the configuration file, completely quit Claude Desktop and restart it. The application needs to restart to load the new configuration and start the MCP server.

Upon successful restart, click the "Add files, connectors, and more /" indicator ![](https://mintcdn.com/mcp/cpXzQjUOzyH0mCNH/images/claude-add-files-connectors-and-more.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=cpXzQjUOzyH0mCNH\&q=85\&s=53acf21f6807dd5323b70b84b5d98d8a) in the bottom-left corner of the conversation input box:

![Claude Desktop interface showing MCP server indicator](https://mintcdn.com/mcp/akpggzunDlIcY2im/images/quickstart-slider.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=akpggzunDlIcY2im\&q=85\&s=a1ebd4259cff2a7472171885f2edc035)

Click on this indicator, then move the mouse over "Connectors" and click "Manage connectors". Select "filesystem" from the connector list to view the Filesystem Server's available tools:

![Available filesystem tools in Claude Desktop](https://mintcdn.com/mcp/cpXzQjUOzyH0mCNH/images/quickstart-tools.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=cpXzQjUOzyH0mCNH\&q=85\&s=212a63d76daba170d52db0d2f6f582be)

If the Filesystem Server doesn't connect, refer to the [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting) section for debugging steps.

## Using the Filesystem Server

With the Filesystem Server connected, Claude can now interact with your file system. Try these example requests to explore the capabilities:

### File Management Examples

* **"Can you write a poem and save it to my desktop?"** - Claude will compose a poem and create a new text file on your desktop
* **"What work-related files are in my downloads folder?"** - Claude will scan your downloads and identify work-related documents
* **"Please organize all images on my desktop into a new folder called 'Images'"** - Claude will create a folder and move image files into it

### How Approval Works

Before executing any file system operation, Claude will request your approval. This ensures you maintain control over all actions:

![Claude requesting approval to perform a file operation](https://mintcdn.com/mcp/4ZXF1PrDkEaJvXpn/images/quickstart-approve.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=4ZXF1PrDkEaJvXpn\&q=85\&s=98cc6e9dfe885fbd6e9bfae40601e494)

Review each request carefully before approving. You can always deny a request if you're not comfortable with the proposed action.

## Troubleshooting

If you encounter issues setting up or using the Filesystem Server, these solutions address common problems:

> [accordion] Server not showing up in Claude / hammer icon missing
>
> 1. Restart Claude Desktop completely
> 2. Check your `claude_desktop_config.json` file syntax
> 3. Make sure the file paths included in `claude_desktop_config.json` are valid and that they are absolute and not relative
> 4. Look at [logs](#getting-logs-from-claude-desktop) to see why the server is not connecting
> 5. In your command line, try manually running the server (replacing `username` as you did in `claude_desktop_config.json`) to see if you get any errors:
>
> ```bash macOS/Linux theme={null}
> npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem /Users/username/Desktop /Users/username/Downloads
> ```
>
> ```powershell Windows theme={null}
> npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem C:\Users\username\Desktop C:\Users\username\Downloads
> ```

> [accordion] Getting logs from Claude Desktop
>
> Claude.app logging related to MCP is written to log files in:
>
> * macOS: `~/Library/Logs/Claude`
>
> * Windows: `%APPDATA%\Claude\logs`
>
> * Linux: `~/.config/Claude/logs`
>
> * `mcp.log` will contain general logging about MCP connections and connection failures.
>
> * Files named `mcp-server-SERVERNAME.log` will contain the stderr output from the named server. Stdio servers may use stderr for all their logging, so these files are not limited to errors.
>
> You can run the following command to list recent logs and follow along with any new ones (on Windows, it will only show recent logs):
>
> ```bash macOS theme={null}
> tail -n 20 -f ~/Library/Logs/Claude/mcp*.log
> ```
>
> ```bash Linux theme={null}
> tail -n 20 -f ~/.config/Claude/logs/mcp*.log
> ```
>
> ```powershell Windows theme={null}
> type "$env:AppData\Claude\logs\mcp*.log"
> ```

> [accordion] Tool calls failing silently
>
> If Claude attempts to use the tools but they fail:
>
> 1. Check Claude's logs for errors
> 2. Verify your server builds and runs without errors
> 3. Try restarting Claude Desktop

> [accordion] None of this is working. What do I do?
>
> Please refer to our [debugging guide](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/tools/debugging.md) for better debugging tools and more detailed guidance.

> [accordion] ENOENT error and `$\{APPDATA\}` in paths on Windows
>
> If your configured server fails to load, and you see within its logs an error referring to `${APPDATA}` within a path, you may need to add the expanded value of `%APPDATA%` to your `env` key in `claude_desktop_config.json`:
>
> ```json theme={null}
> {
>   "mcpServers": {
>     "filesystem": {
>       "command": "npx",
>       "args": [
>         "-y",
>         "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem",
>         "C:\\Users\\username\\Desktop",
>         "C:\\Users\\username\\Downloads"
>       ],
>       "env": {
>         "APPDATA": "C:\\Users\\username\\AppData\\Roaming"
>       }
>     }
>   }
> }
> ```
>
> With this change in place, launch Claude Desktop once again.
>
> > [!WARNING]
> >
> > **npm should be installed globally**
> >
> > The `npx` command may continue to fail if you have not installed npm globally. If npm is already installed globally, you will find `%APPDATA%\npm` exists on your system. If not, you can install npm globally by running the following command:
> >
> > ```bash theme={null}
> > npm install -g npm
> > ```

## Next Steps

Now that you've successfully connected Claude Desktop to a local MCP server, explore these options to expand your setup:

> [card] [Explore other servers](https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io/)
>
> Browse the servers published to the MCP Registry

> [card] [Build your own server](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/develop/build-server.md)
>
> Create custom MCP servers tailored to your specific workflows and
> integrations

> [card] [Connect to remote servers](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/develop/connect-remote-servers.md)
>
> Learn how to connect Claude to remote MCP servers for cloud-based tools and
> services

> [card] [Understand the protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/learn/architecture.md)
>
> Dive deeper into how MCP works and its architecture

## How MCP server updates reach users (checked against docs and source as of 2026-11-20)

**Bottom line:** With `npx -y @discourse-graphs/mcp@latest`, current npm checks the registry on every launch and installs a new version if one exists. The update takes effect only when the client restarts the stdio process: quit and reopen Claude Desktop, use `/mcp` → Reconnect (or restart) in Claude Code, or restart Codex. Nothing tells the user an update exists. If you need to detect stale clients, your server has to do it itself.

### 1. npx / uvx mechanics
- **(a) How the update arrives.** I read the current npm source (`workspaces/libnpmexec/lib/index.js`, npm/cli `latest`). Every manifest lookup runs with `preferOnline: true`, so npm revalidates the package metadata with the registry on each launch.
  - **`pkg@latest` (a tag):** npx resolves the tag and compares the resolved tarball with the copy in `~/.npm/_npx/<hash>`. If they differ, it installs the new version. This is the same in the v9.9.3, v10.2.0, v10.9.0 and current source.
  - **Bare `pkg` (no version):** in the npx cache it is treated the same way (`npxByNameOnly`). But if the package is installed in the client's working-directory project or globally, npx runs that copy, which may be old. npx docs: "Package names provided without a specifier will be matched with whatever version exists in the local project." So `@latest` protects you from an old `npm i -g` copy; a bare name does not. https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npx
  - **Exact pin (`pkg@1.2.3`):** never changes. Updating means editing the config.
  - **Ranges (`pkg@^1`):** older npm could keep a stale cached match. Fixed Feb 2025 (commit 8461186). https://github.com/npm/cli/issues/7838
  - **Old reports:** the many "npx serves a stale copy" threads mostly concern npm 6/7 or ranges. https://github.com/npm/cli/issues/1935
  - **Cache key:** the `_npx` folder is a hash of the spec string, so `pkg` and `pkg@latest` get separate cache folders.
- **(b) What the user does:** restart the client. Nothing else.
- **(c) Speed and reliability:** the next launch after you publish. Not verified:
  - What happens offline. My expectation is that npm fails or falls back to its HTTP cache; I did not test it.
  - How long the npm registry's CDN keeps serving the old package metadata after a publish. A related `npm pack` stale-metadata bug was fixed in March 2026 (https://github.com/npm/cli/issues/9045).
- **Costs:** every launch makes a network call, which adds startup time. Codex's default `startup_timeout_sec` is 10 seconds.
- **Risk:** `@latest` delivers breaking releases instantly and you cannot hold users back.
- **(d) Non-technical users:** good. Nothing to do beyond a restart.
- **uvx:** reuses the cached copy "unless a different version is requested". `pkg@latest` refreshes the cache. If the user ran `uv tool install`, that installed version wins unless `@latest` is given. So for uvx, use `@latest` explicitly. https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/tools/

### 2. When the update takes effect (all clients)
The client starts the stdio process when it launches. A new version runs only after that process is restarted.
- **Claude Desktop:** "completely quit Claude Desktop and restart it." https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/develop/connect-local-servers
- **Claude Code:**
  - `/mcp` → **Reconnect** for one server.
  - `/mcp reconnect all` (needs v2.1.284 or later) retries all failed or unauthenticated servers, so I'm not sure it restarts a healthy one.

  - `claude -p` runs pick up the new version on the next run. https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp

  - Watch-out: `startup_readiness = "catalog"` lets a cached tool list satisfy startup while the server connects, so the tool list Codex shows can briefly be older than the running server. https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/extend/mcp?surface=cli

### 3. Claude Desktop extensions (.mcpb)
- **(a) How the update arrives:**
  - Directory extensions "update automatically by default". Privately distributed `.mcpb` files must be "install[ed] manually". https://support.claude.com/en/articles/10949351
  - **Major change, current docs:** "Desktop extension listings in the directory are deprecated, and the directory no longer accepts MCPB submissions. To distribute a local MCP server through the directory, include it in a plugin." https://claude.com/docs/connectors/building/mcpb.md
  - So a new `@discourse-graphs` `.mcpb` would be a manual download. Every update means downloading the new file and double-clicking it again.
- **How updates are signalled:** not documented for privately distributed files. Assume users are never told.
- **(d) Non-technical users:** installing is the easiest of all options (bundled Node, settings form generated from the manifest). Updating is the worst.

### 4. Plugins (the new directory route; Claude Code is documented)
- **(a)** You bump `version` in `plugin.json`, or omit `version` so users track commits. Users get the new copy through background auto-update or by running `/plugin marketplace update` or `claude plugin update`.
- **(b) Watch-out:** auto-update is **off by default for third-party marketplaces**, and `marketplace.json` has no field to turn it on. Each user toggles it in `/plugin` → Marketplaces, or an admin sets it in managed settings.
- **(c) Watch-out:** if you keep the same `version` string, users never get new commits.
- **Partial lever:** a plugin's MCP config could still point at `npx …@latest`, which avoids depending on plugin updates for the server code.
- https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/host-marketplace.md
- Not verified: whether Anthropic's official directory marketplace auto-updates by default.

### 5. Registries and catalogs
- **Official MCP Registry:**
  - Still "in preview". It holds metadata only: `server.json` points at the npm package. Every publish needs a new, unique version string, and published entries cannot be changed.
  - Docs say it is "not intended to be directly consumed by host applications". Aggregators are expected to sync roughly hourly.
  - I found **no client that auto-updates from it**. Publishing helps people discover the server; it does not deliver updates.
  - https://modelcontextprotocol.io/registry/about, https://modelcontextprotocol.io/registry/versioning
- **Docker MCP Catalog / Toolkit:**
  - Docker builds and signs local servers in the `mcp/` namespace. Teams can "control which server versions" they use through custom catalogs.
  - New listings appear within about 24 hours of approval.
  - The docs don't cover how image updates reach users (tags, pull behaviour). Unverified. https://docs.docker.com/ai/mcp-catalog-and-toolkit/catalog/
- **Smithery:**
  - Its hosted services, CLI and SDKs **shut down on 2026-10-31**. It is now only a non-proxied directory, run by Arcade.
  - Don't build on it. https://smithery.ai/future

### 6. Remote (Streamable HTTP) servers
- **(a)** You deploy, and every user is on the new code immediately. Anthropic lists "Centralized updates pushed to all users" as a reason to choose remote over MCPB (mcpb.md, link above).
- **What clients cache:**
  - The tool list, until a `list_changed` notification or a reconnect. Claude Code keeps the last list if a refresh fails.
  - Codex can start from a cached tool list (see §2).
- **(b)** At most a reconnect.
- **(d)** Best fit, but it means running a hosted service with OAuth, which conflicts with your local session-state design.

### 7. Git-checkout installs
Updating means `git pull`, `pnpm install` if dependencies changed, then restart the client. Speed depends entirely on the user remembering to do it. Fine for contributors; not workable for non-technical users. (No source needed.)

### 8. What other servers do
- **Playwright MCP:** every client snippet uses `npx @playwright/mcp@latest`. https://github.com/microsoft/playwright-mcp
- **Sentry:**
  - Its main offering is the remote `https://mcp.sentry.dev`.
  - Local use now goes through the Sentry CLI's `sentry mcp`.
  - `npx @sentry/mcp-server@latest` is labelled "Legacy". https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-mcp
- **GitHub:**
  - Recommends the remote server first. The local server is a fallback for clients without remote support.
  - The local Docker image `ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server` is untagged in the examples, with no update guidance.
  - Renamed tools keep their old names "as aliases for backward compatibility".
  - https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server
- **Figma:** not verified.
- **Update warnings:** I found **no** popular server with a built-in "you're out of date" warning or minimum-version check. Not found, not proven absent.
  - If you want one, a self-built option: the server compares its own version with the npm registry at startup and puts a notice in its `instructions` or tool results.

### Recommendation for `@discourse-graphs/mcp`
- Keep `npx -y …@latest`. Never tell users to `npm i -g`.
- Restart the client is the only user step; document it per client.
- Keep the session-state file format backward-compatible across versions, because users jump to new versions with no warning and you can't hold them back.
- Add a server-side minimum-version check, so a user who is behind gets told.
- An `.mcpb` makes installing easier but makes updating manual. A plugin needs the user to turn on auto-update. A remote server is the only option where updates reach every user with nothing on their side.

### Couldn't verify
- npx behaviour offline.
- How long the npm registry CDN serves old package metadata after a publish.
- How Claude Desktop signals updates for extensions.
- Default auto-update for the official Anthropic plugin directory.
- Cursor / VS Code restart UX.
- How Docker catalog image updates reach users.
- Figma's approach.

## How MCP server updates reach users (checked against docs and source as of 2026-11-20)

**Bottom line:** With `npx -y @discourse-graphs/mcp@latest`, current npm checks the registry on every launch and installs a new version if one exists. The update takes effect only when the client restarts the stdio process: quit and reopen Claude Desktop, use `/mcp` → Reconnect (or restart) in Claude Code, or restart Codex. Nothing tells the user an update exists. If you need to detect stale clients, your server has to do it itself.

### 1. npx / uvx mechanics
- **(a) How the update arrives.** I read the current npm source (`workspaces/libnpmexec/lib/index.js`, npm/cli `latest`). Every manifest lookup runs with `preferOnline: true`, so npm revalidates the package metadata with the registry on each launch.
  - **`pkg@latest` (a tag):** npx resolves the tag and compares the resolved tarball with the copy in `~/.npm/_npx/<hash>`. If they differ, it installs the new version. This is the same in the v9.9.3, v10.2.0, v10.9.0 and current source.
  - **Bare `pkg` (no version):** in the npx cache it is treated the same way (`npxByNameOnly`). But if the package is installed in the client's working-directory project or globally, npx runs that copy, which may be old. npx docs: "Package names provided without a specifier will be matched with whatever version exists in the local project." So `@latest` protects you from an old `npm i -g` copy; a bare name does not. https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npx
  - **Exact pin (`pkg@1.2.3`):** never changes. Updating means editing the config.
  - **Ranges (`pkg@^1`):** older npm could keep a stale cached match. Fixed Feb 2025 (commit 8461186). https://github.com/npm/cli/issues/7838
  - **Old reports:** the many "npx serves a stale copy" threads mostly concern npm 6/7 or ranges. https://github.com/npm/cli/issues/1935
  - **Cache key:** the `_npx` folder is a hash of the spec string, so `pkg` and `pkg@latest` get separate cache folders.
- **(b) What the user does:** restart the client. Nothing else.
- **(c) Speed and reliability:** the next launch after you publish. Not verified:
  - What happens offline. My expectation is that npm fails or falls back to its HTTP cache; I did not test it.
  - How long the npm registry's CDN keeps serving the old package metadata after a publish. A related `npm pack` stale-metadata bug was fixed in March 2026 (https://github.com/npm/cli/issues/9045).
- **Costs:** every launch makes a network call, which adds startup time. Codex's default `startup_timeout_sec` is 10 seconds.
- **Risk:** `@latest` delivers breaking releases instantly and you cannot hold users back.
- **(d) Non-technical users:** good. Nothing to do beyond a restart.
- **uvx:** reuses the cached copy "unless a different version is requested". `pkg@latest` refreshes the cache. If the user ran `uv tool install`, that installed version wins unless `@latest` is given. So for uvx, use `@latest` explicitly. https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/tools/
